rationale:
Evidence. Iteration 10 (wheel_track 0.10, otherwise iteration 9) scored 95.95, against 98.24 for iteration 9 (wheel_track 0.14). Its dev-track metrics are better on three of four counts: line loss cleared to 0 on every track (0.6 per trial on slalom at 0.14). Progress rose on every track: oval 0.390 (0.373), s-bend 0.178 (0.160), slalom 0.110 (0.101). Slalom max_error fell from 0.0623 to 0.0650, which is worse, but this is still a pinned-limit failure. The whole score gap comes from one lucky oval finish at 0.14 (945.9 on one trial), which gave the 0.14 design a mean of 184 on oval against 165 at 0.10. Oval max_error was 0.0610 at 0.14 and 0.0613 at 0.10, so neither is inside the limit. The plan's fallback trigger (slalom progress falling or line loss rising at 0.10) did not fire, since slalom progress rose and line loss cleared.

Decision. Submit the iteration-10 design unchanged (wheel_track 0.10, base_speed 0.9, kd 0.3, ki 0.4, kp 2.0, search_right, sensor y 0.05, x -0.07 to 0.07, sensor_size 0.016). It is the only raced design with zero line loss on every development track and the highest progress on all three. I am not changing base_speed or any other field now. Speed 1.1 to 0.9 was the only change that moved progress materially, but raising speed to 1.0 is untested and max_error is still at the limit, so an untested step in the final iteration carries too much risk.

Expected result. Similar to iteration 10 on the unseen track: no line loss, progress near 0.11 to 0.39 depending on track shape, and a finish only if the course is gentle. Hypotheses: H1, the narrower track gives more turn authority, which is why slalom line loss clears. H2, max_error stays at the 0.060 to 0.065 limit on every track, so the excursion is not driven by the drivetrain or the feedback gains. Measurements wanted: max_error, line_loss_events and progress per track, plus completion_time for any finish, so the next team can judge whether the 0.10 track width or the lucky 0.14 finish is the real driver.
